sm: President Trump arrives in Asia for high-stakes talks with China's Xi Jinping, along with a trilateral meeting involving Russia's Vladimir Putin. Hosts Georgia Howe and John Vikli open the Tuesday, November 17th show with the day's top stories. In New York, Mayor Mamdani unveils a plan to send unarmed citizens to help manage protests, through a new community dialogue and de-escalation division. Meanwhile, Democrats are preparing sweeping investigations, and a senator vows to use every tool of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations to make sure justice is served.

China and national security expert Steve Yates explains the stops on Trump's itinerary, starting with the ASEAN summit in the Philippines. He says visiting the Philippines matters because China has been aggressively encroaching on its waters, and it is good to reassure an ally before meeting Xi. He expects the China meeting to be mostly theater, with Trump raising nuclear arms control with Russia and China. Leaders will meet again at the G20 in Miami in December, so he expects little progress on AI. He warns the biggest pitfall would be conceding on Taiwan, which is central to advanced chips, and he thinks China will avoid awkward topics like the Nvidia spy scandal. On Kim Jong-un, he calls the idea a classic Trump surprise, noting Kim dislikes flying, and Trump said it is up to Xi. Asked about recent outages at United Airlines, the FAA and Microsoft, he avoids grand conclusions but says the accumulation should push the country to win the AI race, invest in resilient infrastructure, and cooperate with trustworthy partners while competing fairly with China.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani announces he is disbanding the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, the unit handling counterterrorism, major crimes and riot response, keeping a campaign promise. Daily Wire reporter Brea Stoll says his video drew 19 million views in hours. He argues counterterrorism officers should not be at protests, but she notes New York is always a terrorism concern, citing two teenagers who threw Molotov cocktails into a protest months ago. In the unit's place, a civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division will engage protesters. Those workers are unarmed, have no pepper spray and no arrest powers. A network of officers called FAST can be called to make arrests, though it is unclear whether they will be at protests from the start. Mamdani says there will be no long guns, tear gas, kettling or pepper spray at First Amendment events. The police union says this endangers officers and the public, but Commissioner Jessica Tisch supports it, saying headcount will not fall and counterterrorism officers will move to the department's terrorism unit. Stoll adds that Tisch is outspoken and may speak up if problems arise.

Daily Wire reporter Megan Basham says Democrats, claiming a midterm mandate, plan investigations across multiple committees in both chambers when they take over in January. Congressman Robert Garcia, who posted lawyer up on election night, and incoming Judiciary chair Jamie Raskin target Trump family business dealings, the Epstein investigation, immigration enforcement, corporate donations to the White House ballroom project, and impeachment hearings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The big change is subpoena power to compel documents and testimony, backed by court action. Senator Richard Blumenthal also points to coordinating with blue state attorneys general, since Trump's immunity ruling does not apply to state prosecutors, and Democrats want records from private businesses. Attorney General Todd Blanche says supporters of Trump need not comply. White House counsel Will Scharf warns some probes could cross into criminality and says the administration will not be cowed. U.S. Attorney Aaron Wright has told Senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal to preserve documents, saying they could face conspiracy investigations if they punish private citizens for associating with the president.
